utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask the Registrar to call the case number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Williamson, Ms. Sutherland, Mr. Waespi and Mr. Vos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Toma Fila. I appear with Ms. Lopicic and Mr. Petkovic representing the defendant, Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask Mr. Dokmanovic if he can hear me. Thank you. All right. Before we call the first witness, I would like to suggest that we should deal with a few legal housekeeping matters. First of all, the court is grateful to the Prosecutor for submitting two documents. One is the list of witnesses, and the other one are the two documents concerning the agreement about the evacuation of Ilok. Now, as for the first document, we have seen that the Prosecutor kindly set out also the estimated length of examination of each witness. I wonder whether those rough estimates of the length of the examination of each witness includes the cross-examination? I would say so, judging from your calculation of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are, yes, as you have indicated, very rough estimates, but we believed that this would encompass both the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the court is wondering whether we could try to reduce the length of examination for some witnesses who might appear to be less important, and we would like to make a few suggestions concerning particularly, I think, seven witnesses. We were wondering whether, for witness number 1 -- I am thinking, of course, by the way, of the list which is at the back of the documents submitted by the Prosecutor, the confidential document submitted on 29th January, and I will indicate the various witnesses only by their number, so as to avoid any confusion or any disclosure of names of protected witnesses. Now, our suggestions would be as follows: now, could we reduce for witness 1 the possible length of examination from two and a half hours to two hours? Do you think this is feasible? Shall I first of all maybe go through the various witnesses and then you tell me whether it is acceptable. Witness number 2, can we go down from two hours to one and a half hours; number 3, reduce from two hours to one hour; number 4, instead of an hour and a half, one hour; number 6, instead of two hours, one hour; number 9, one hour instead of two; number 10, one hour instead of two. Of course, I appreciate that it is rather difficult for the Prosecutor to make any promise, but this we are indicating as a sort of goal which we should try to achieve in the interest of a fair and expeditious trial, so I wonder whether we could make an effort so as to reduce the length of examination-in-chief and cross-examination of these seven witnesses, so that because in this case we could gain about five and a half hours this week, and we would be able to maybe call three more witnesses. The Prosecutor, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does your Honour wish me to respond now to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, it is very difficult to reduce these periods of time. I mean, this is a good faith estimate of time. The first witness is important because that witness covers a broad spectrum of events which is introductory and substantive leading through to setting the scene and then leading to the substantive events. Witness 10 probably will not even come so you have saved two hours there anyway and you have probably saved a great deal more because we will probably lose quite a few more witnesses as time goes. I will ask my colleague Mr. Williamson to speak to other witnesses, but it seems to us, your Honours, that the witnesses will only testify to that which is relevant, and if there is something which is not relevant, then we will do our best to avoid that, but we are anxious not to have the witnesses go for an extensive period of time. We have done something unusual here. We have attempted to calculate cross-examination time, which is in a sense presumptuous on our part, but we tried to give the court an overall estimate of the period of time we would take. We have, of course, no control over cross-examination. I will ask Mr. Williamson to speak to the other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you indicated early on, this is a very rough estimate. It is our belief that some of the witnesses that appear on the list may actually be less than the time indicated, some may be more. But as Mr. Niemann has said, we have made a good faith effort to condense it as much as possible. I think that we are presenting a very efficient, concise case in this matter, and even if we stick to the schedule that we are, this case will move along much faster than any of the other cases that have been heard before the court thus far. In relation to the other specific witnesses you mentioned, number 2, number 3 and number 4 all relate to events at the hospital. Again, they are setting the stage for what occurs later on, and we feel that their testimony is important in establishing some of the other elements that we are required to prove in terms of the classification of victims, the armed conflict, the nature of the conflict, and in fact, address some of the issues which have been denied by the Defence in terms of their points denied in the indictment. We feel that it is our obligation to prove every point that they have denied, and they have provided a very thorough listing of basically everything that they have denied in the indictment, and it is our obligation to prove this. Since we bear the burden we feel like we have to do it in the best way we can. We will make every effort to keep these witnesses as short as possible and to the point, but I think you will find that as we move along that many of them will be shorter than the times that we have anticipated, but some of them may be longer. On that issue, witness number 9, which we had previously indicated for two hours, we believe may actually be longer than that because this was based on what we have in terms of witness statements for each of these persons. As witnesses arrive here and we have an opportunity to sit down and talk with the witnesses, some of them are able to see for the first time video material that we have or documents that we have. We find that they have other information which we were not anticipating them having to testify about. In the case of witness 9, there will be some video footage that we had no intention of offering, but after he has seen this we believe that it is relevant, that it helps to clarify his testimony, and that it will help the court to have a clear picture of what is going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am sorry, just a moment, your Honour. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: One possibility, your Honours, that occurred to me while we were discussing this matter is if we were to tender the statements as evidence in the proceedings that may assist in reducing the time, so if the Defence has no objection to them being tendered as evidence in the proceedings, some introductory material can be eliminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This would apply to how many witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We could tender all the statements as we go through and we could possibly reduce it that way, but it, of course, is entirely a matter for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes? Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I first say that, referring to the evidence mentioned by the Prosecutor, a part refers to the operations of the JNA, about the hospital and other things. These matters are not directly linked to Dokmanovic, so I do not even know if there will be any cross-examination. If any, it will be reduced to one or two questions. What we are interested in are witnesses 12 and 13, and for them I will need a little more time. Secondly, the Defence is not denying the fact that there was an armed conflict. What we are denying is that it was an international armed conflict. The Defence is not denying that the hospital was destroyed. The Defence has no intention of defending the JNA, but Slavko Dokmanovic. That is why I shall be as brief as possible and concise as possible and focus exclusively on Slavko Dokmanovic, who was not an officer or a reserve officer, who was in fact not a member of the army at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, but may I ask you about your position concerning the suggestion made a few minutes ago by the Prosecution, to the effect that the witness statements could be tendered as evidence? Of course, if you do not object. What is your position on this matter? The Prosecution witness statements would be provided to the court and be regarded as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would prefer to hear those witnesses, only they could be more concise. Because in the statements there is nothing about Dokmanovic. They were taken before Dokmanovic was indicted and therefore we have to know whether they have any knowledge about him, whether that knowledge is positive or negative, because we will see that all those statements refer to JNA officers, if I am not mistaken, and at the time Dokmanovic was not an indictee. It is before 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But if I understood the Prosecutor correctly, he meant to say that in this case, of course, the production of the witness statements as evidence would not mean that the witnesses are not heard by the court, simply that we could focus our questions on some specific questions, so of course, it goes without saying that we will have to call all these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise, your Honour. I apologise. I misunderstood. In that case I have no objection. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I should like to say, your Honour, just in light of that, that our position is the same, in the sense that we do not want it in any way interpreted that because we are advancing the proposition that these statements could become evidence, that somehow or other that will mean, then, that the Defence or indeed the Prosecution will automatically be in a position of tendering statements without calling the witnesses as evidence, because I should foreshadow that we would object to statements being tendered in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, one last point relating to the list of witnesses produced by the Prosecution is as follows; I think -- the court has not received statements made by four witnesses, so Witness K and three other witnesses. I wonder whether the -- I assume the Prosecution has already disclosed those statements to the Defence, but I wonder whether the court as well could receive a copy of those four statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the statement of Witness K should have been tendered both to the court and to the Defence. I believe the Defence has this. We can double-check. In relation to the other witnesses, could you indicate which witnesses those were? I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This is Vladimir Veber, Katica Zara and Dragan Zera. These are the witnesses to be called in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. In relation to those three witnesses, we have not taken statements from those persons, and we do not anticipate taking statements. These are relatives of persons who were killed at Ovcara. Their testimony will be relatively brief but we can certainly prepare a summary of the main theme of their testimony and provide that both to the Defence and the court in advance of them appearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I have a list of six witnesses to be called in February/March. Again, their statements have not been provided to the court. Shall I read out the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I know which witnesses you are indicating. This would appear on the... The first witness which indicates, "February /March". Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And then the four witnesses which are all marked with, "February /March", as the potential date of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, but to expedite matters I suggest to give both the Defence and the Prosecution a copy of my list as a tentative guide of the various witnesses for whom we do not have any statements, so -- otherwise we waste a lot of time. May I move on to a second problem, and here I turn to the Defence, and I wonder whether the Defence would object to the two documents produced by the Prosecution and concerning the evacuation of Ilok, being formally exhibited, thus becoming part of our record. The so-called agreement and the ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not received the statement of Witness K; just like you have not received it, I have not either. That is number one. Number two, as regards these two documents, and another twenty or so documents that I received from the Prosecutor this morning, that they should be considered exhibits, I fully agree with them, including those given to me by the Prosecutor this morning. They can be considered as evidence. I also agree that we are given a rough outline of what the witnesses would say. It is not necessary to have the statement in extenso.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, may I suggest that we now formally regard the -- as exhibits and we have to give a number -- the agreement to be found in the document filed by the Prosecution on 29th January, this is the agreement concerning the evacuation of Ilok. This would be what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We will mark it as Prosecution exhibit number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecution exhibit number 5. Then the so-called, "ultimatum", of 28th September 1991 to be found in the same document. This would become Prosecution's exhibit number 6. May I now turn to the Prosecution and ask whether the Prosecution agrees to the meteorological report produced by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good. So this can be again regarded as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We will mark that as Defence exhibit number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Number 1. All right. Defence exhibit number 1. A few minor problems which, however, must be disposed of quickly before we move to our first witness. Now, again, I will turn to the -- to both parties, actually, because the question I would like to ask is about the 45 so-called, "minor Defence witnesses". You will remember that mention was made in our previous hearings of these so-called 45 minor Defence witnesses and at some stage I ask the two parties whether they could reach some sort of agreement on their statements, because I remember the Defence counsel had asked that all of them be heard through deposition, they are not prepared to come to court, so he insisted that deposition should be made for these statements and so at that stage I suggested to try to see whether they could reach some sort of an agreement. I wonder whether such agreement has been reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have had discussions with the Defence, but basically, the position is not any different to what it was on the previous occasion when we were in court and that is that I do not think it is a case of deposition, it is a case of the Prosecution interviewing the witnesses and seeing whether there is any aspect of the evidence that we can agree to so that it may not be necessary to call the witness at all. The exercise of taking depositions is as difficult and costly as bringing the witnesses here to court, so we had agreed that we would endeavour to go to Belgrade and interview the 45 witnesses and see whether or not there is any points on which we can agree and if we can agree then we have no objection to some form of admission being formally tendered in the proceedings. If we cannot agree, then the issue then falls back to the witnesses being called before the proceedings in the ordinary way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is our intention to endeavour to do this before the close of the Prosecution case or at least at the end of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as a last point, let me just give you the tentative schedule for the next three months, the schedule of our hearings, because there have been, I think, some slight variations. Now you know, of course, that we are going to sit here until Wednesday of next week, so eight working days, but then we will resume our hearings in March and there will be hearings from 16th-20th March, so five working days. In April from 20th-29th of April, so eight working days, and then in May, from 18th-29th of May, ten working days. We will try to see whether we can get the courtroom for a few more days so that we can have, say, maybe one week, one more week either in April or May but this is rather difficult because of the present constraints, logistical constraints. All right. Now, we could probably now call the first witness. Before doing so, let me try to sum up one point which was argued this morning about the witness statements being tendered as evidence. I assume that the Prosecution meant to say that as the witness comes here then he may decide to tender the witness statement as evidence so that the examination and the cross-examination may focus on some specific points, and the court will not have to go into matters which are covered by the witness statement, so as -- so therefore, the production of the witness statement as evidence will take place when -- if and when the witness comes here. Is it correct? This would be my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The course that I would propose would be to show the witness the statement and ask whether that is the signature which appears. Of course it is not in the language of the accused so the witness cannot say that yes, that is her statement because it will be inspect the English language, or his statement, but we would be seeking to tender the totality of the document as evidence so it would not be as though we are merely tendering part of it in relation to what the witness might say in the witness-box or otherwise. We would say that the whole of the statement becomes an exhibit and is evidence without restriction. On that basis, we would try and reduce the amount of time spent with the witness on what I might call, "introductory matters". If they are covered in the statement we can move directly into the pith and substance of the statement rather than dealing with the important, relevant, admissible preliminary matters, but avoid going through -- spending the time in court going through those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You referred only to those witnesses whom you intend to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So not all the statements which have been produced to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. Those ones will be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And I see that the Defence council does not object to this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, on the contrary. I just wish to be of assistance to Mr. Niemann. All those statements have already been translated into Serbo-Croatian so the witnesses can identify the translation as being the original, and that would solve the problem. Secondly, I have brought what you asked me to bring, so I should like to present it to you for your consideration. (Handed). These are documents related to the army, and I have also submitted the 74 Yugoslav constitution translated into English. I have given a copy to Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do not have a copy of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, there should be copies also. Do you have a copy for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise. I do not have a copy. I just wanted you to have a look whether that is what you were expecting from me and if that is so, then I can make a copy. That is why I produced only one copy. I apologise, but I just wanted to check whether that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We can look during the coffee break and then we will let you know. Thank you. We could now call the first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before I do that, there was a matter which did arise out of the previous occasion which, if I may clarify; your Honour has asked for a memorandum on two issues; the international armed conflict and on the issue of cumulative and alternative charging. That, of course, is not an issue in the proceedings as yet. It may well become so, but it is not. So if we were in the process of preparing a memorandum on this, I assume your Honours are not going to rule on it because it is not an issue, and it would be, in a sense, an extension of my opening address. That would be the way I assume we are to deal with it, because your Honours have not been asked to rule on it by either party yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I did not understand what -- so are you asking for an extension of the time limit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. Your Honour asked for a memorandum on international armed conflict and one on cumulative charging. The parties are joined. There is no issue between the parties as such, so I would just clarify the basis upon which it is being made available. I assume it is being made available on the basis that it is an extension of my opening address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If that is the case, that is fine. We anticipate being in a position to provide that to your Honour as before at the end of this week, early next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. It will assist the court in assessing this matter's legal issues. Thank you. Right. So you may call the first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I call Vesna Bosanac. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please make the formal declaration? VESNA BOSANAC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you a qualified medical practitioner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you director of the Vukovar General Hospital and do you still have that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in particular, were you a director of that hospital in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In particular, the latter part of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was director from 24th July until 20th November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, was the Vukovar hospital bombed during the course of the conflict in August, September, October and November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Several times, and on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And could you describe very briefly to the court the nature of the attack upon the hospital? What sort of weapons were used against the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, the shelling of the hospital occurred in August 1991 when, on 15th August a shell hit the management building. Also, shells fell on the main hospital building. The fire came from the other side of the Danube and the roof was targeted, so that the surgery wards had to be moved to lower floors and anti-atomic shelter provided. On 24th August was the first time when the hospital was shelled from the air with aeroplanes, and as of 14th September it was shelled daily until 17th November a total of some between 60 and 200 projectiles of various kinds, shells and bombs were dropped on the hospital using various types of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I mean, who was firing upon the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fire came from positions held by the Yugoslav People's Army from the other bank of the Danube, from the Vojvodina side, also from the direction of Negoslavci and Borovo Selo. Vukovar was completely surrounded for three months, and there were cannon and tanks around the centre of the town belonging to the Yugoslav People's Army, JNA planes were also almost daily flying over the hospital and shelling the hospital and other buildings in the surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know why Vukovar was being attacked by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the 1991 war many towns were attacked. I do not know with certainty, but I assume that Vukovar was being attacked in order to gain control of it which, in fact, happened between 18th and 20th November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Previous to this attack had Vukovar experienced hostilities and difficulties amongst the population of that city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in Vukovar for 17 years as a doctor. Vukovar is a small town in the south east of Croatia on the right bank of the Danube. Before the war it had a population of 45,000, and the entire region was inhabited by representatives of various ethnic groups. The 1991 elections, it emerged that there were 23 ethnicities populating the area. The Croats constituted 43 per cent, the Serbs 38 per cent. There were quite a large percentage of Yugoslavs, about 12 per cent. These were children of mixed marriages who declared their nationality as being Yugoslav, and there were representatives of other ethnic groups, Ruthenes, Hungarians, Ukrainians, Albanians in smaller percentages, therefore a large number of ethnic groups were represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that the hospital which you were a director of was attacked. Was there any military installation or other reason that you know of why the hospital itself would have been attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were never any military installations in the hospital. I think the hospital was attacked more than other parts of the city, though I can conclude from the fierce attacks, in spite of all the protests I made to protect the hospital, that it was attacked because in the hospital, which was operational, everyone, both the police and the army and the people had support. There were doctors, there were nurses, and they could be sure that they would be helped should they be injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the hospital have any markings or other indicia on the hospital itself to indicate that it was in fact a hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the old hospital building where the department for infectious lung diseases was situated, there was a large red cross and as we could not climb on to the roof of the new building, then on the lawn between the old and new building we spread out a large sheet, a white sheet with the red cross which was 20 metres in diameter so it was clearly visible. But in spite of these signs, shells were falling in the garden and airforce shells as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned 24th August 1991. Was that an occasion when four JNA soldiers were brought into the hospital for treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a checkpoint of the Yugoslav People's Army between Borovo Naselje and Borovo Selo because troops were passing through town and personnel carriers, regularly, and they came across mines. Four soldiers were brought in, two of whom were lightly injured, one was seriously injured and the other had very heavy burns all over his body from the explosion. They were admitted to the hospital that morning. They were given all necessary medical treatment in line with the principles of medicine and ethics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did the local captain of the JNA, Captain Ristic come to you or ring you and be requested that they be turned over to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He called me up by telephone and asked that the soldiers be brought to the barracks which was in the southern part of the city. I opposed this, and said it was not advisable. It was not in their interest. They were still receiving infusion, that they could be given proper treatment in the hospital and that it was not suitable for them to be transported or to be treated in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, notwithstanding the medical advice that you gave Captain Ristic, did they insist upon him, these soldiers being taken out of your hospital and did that, in fact, occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he insisted, but I said that I could not do it because there was absolutely no medical or ethical justification. However, about half an hour later the chief of police called me up and asked that we prepare the soldiers for evacuation indicating that representatives of the Yugoslav army would come to pick them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did ultimately those representatives come to pick them up? Those representatives of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, shortly after that an armoured personnel carrier entered the hospital compound. I went out because I could not communicate with them because they were inside the carrier, so I knocked on the outside and the lid opened, an officer came out, and I asked why they had come into the hospital, and they said they had come to secure the evacuation of those soldiers. A van belonging to the Yugoslav army also came with a driver. They parked at the entrance to the hospital, and the soldiers who were lightly wounded entered the van whereas those who were more seriously wounded were put in an ambulance. I asked the driver where he was taking them. He said he did not know. He was just following orders. One of the more lightly wounded soldiers was from Vukovar and he did not want to go. He wanted to stay, but the driver had received orders to take them away and they did. One of our nurses called Janiza Janko. She went with the ambulance and when she came back she said she saw many people in the barracks, helicopters, TV reporters, they were all waiting to evacuate the soldiers from Vukovar to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, once the -- well, firstly, do you know of any reason why it would have been necessary to come to the hospital with an armoured personnel carrier? Was there any military threat to the JNA when they came to your hospital, that you know of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And after these men had been removed, did the shelling of your hospital continue or did it abate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It continued. The shelling continued. Actually, the first air-raid on the hospital took place after that, and the shelling continued every day and it was heavier and heavier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you think -- do you know of any reason why the -- I will withdraw that. Did you complain to anyone about the fact that your hospital was being shelled or bombed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I complained every day and several times every day to many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who did you complain to? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, I complained in Zagreb to the Ministry of Health, then to the general headquarters of the Croatian army, and by telephone I got in touch with the general staff in Belgrade via Sarejevo. I also asked to talk on the telephone to the then Prime Minister, Anto Markovic, but I did not manage to speak to him. I spoke to then military deputies of the Yugoslav army on the telephone and they did not believe what I was saying. They kept saying that it was impossible that the hospital was being bombed. Then when I realised that it was no use complaining to anyone and that no one could help me, then through the media in Slovenia I got the telephones and telefaxes of the International Red Cross in Geneva, of UNICEF and all other important politicians in Europe of the day, Mr. Carrington, Genscher, Van den Broek, and I wrote every day. I wrote protests and appeals and asked for assistance and I sent it to the Croatian office attached to the European Mission in the hotel in Zagreb and I asked them to send this further to all these other addresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you say, "the Europe Mission", you are speaking of the European Community Monitoring Mission. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time in the hotel, and in Zagreb there was a Monitoring Mission of the European Community. It was led by Georges Marie Chenu. He was head of this monitoring mission, and during the month of November, as far as I know, negotiations began on establishing a cease-fire in our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, just dealing with those protests you made, did you, apart from making telephone contact, did you also make contact by way of fax?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost every day, or perhaps even twice a day I would describe the current situation in the hospital and in town and I sent telefaxes to the European Mission and asked them to translate this into English and to give these appeals of mine to all members of the European Mission. The telefax in the hospital was out of order because the office building was hit, so every day I either went to the defence headquarters of the town or to the police where the telefax was in operation and that is where I sent these telefaxes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at these bundle of documents that I am now going to give you, please, and would you just look through them? (Handed). Perhaps a copy might be given to Mr. Fila. I think he has already had a copy, but he might need another one, and a copy for your Honours. Doctor, dealing with these documents as a bundle rather than as individual documents, can you just quickly look through the ones that I have now shown you, just to identify that they are the documents that you recognise? Very quickly. I think you have seen them before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are copies of the telefaxes that I wrote and sent to the Croatian office at the European Community Monitoring Mission from October 20th until 15th or 16th November during that most difficult month when the hospital was bombed every day with an average of 100 projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And does your signature and writing appear on a number of these documents, especially where your name is typed, beneath or above that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These are communications that I wrote myself or my secretary wrote them and I would only sign them. And the documents that were translated into English were translated in the Croatian office by the European Mission. Also I sent certain messages by telephone and I asked them to write them down and to send them under my name. Not all the documents I sent are here, but quite a few are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I tender those. Might they be given the next number in order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is exhibit number...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, did you have to do anything with your patients in order to protect them from this constant shelling that was happening to your hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We tried to protect our patients by putting the most difficult patients in the anti-aircraft shelter that was underground, four rooms underground. We had an intensive care unit for the most heavily wounded there, and after the operations, the surgeries that were carried out, they were taken to the anti-nuclear shelter because not a single shell could fall in there. So we had a room there and we also had a delivery room for mothers and their babies that were in incubators. We also had a large room for post-intensive treatment of the wounded, and also a smaller room where the children of the medical staff would spend the night and also nurses from time to time when they were getting some rest. We tried to use all the cellars to a maximum but they were not exactly safe, so sometimes a shell would fall into the cellar of the old building and even the patients were hit by shells. We had very many wounded people. That was the problem. Every day between 16 and 92 wounded people were taken in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On one occasion --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During September we could evacuate the wounded so they could leave Vukovar, but starting from 1st October we could not evacuate anyone any more so there were more and more wounded. After treating them we would send them to civilian shelters. However, just before the occupation of Vukovar at the end of November the number of wounded people came to the figure of 450 and it is certain that there was not even enough room for 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On one occasion around 4th October 1991, did two bombs hit the hospital, one exploding and the other one travelling down through the hospital building itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were two aircraft bombs that hit the hospital. I remember the explosion in surgery on the second floor of the hospital, and the entire hospital, the hallway, everything, was full of dust and gas and everyone panicked. The wounded, the patients, the staff. We thought that the hospital would go on fire because that had already happened several times, but then someone said that a bomb fell directly into the shelter. I went there and at the entrance to the shelter since a big bomb had fallen, I saw that it had fallen directly onto the bed where a patient was lying, by his feet. So this was an elderly man called Pero Vukasin. I heard that he is still alive, that he lives in Vukovar nowadays. So that bomb did not explode but it penetrated the roof and all the floors. It came up to the very entrance to the shelter. The patient was lucky to have survived. He was lucky that it fell by his feet and everybody else was lucky because had that bomb exploded it is certain that the shelter would have exploded and that everybody would have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, I would like you to now look at some photographs, if you would, for me, please. These copies have been made available to your Honours, to the court, and perhaps I can indicate it to the Registrar. It is the one entitled, "Vukovar hospital". Perhaps that could be shown to the witness. You should have that, I understand. (Handed). Thank you. Now, Dr. Bosanac -- perhaps you might assist Dr. Bosanac by setting it up on the overhead projector there. Doctor, what I would like to do is put those particular photographs on the projector that is beside you there and just dealing with them one by one, if you may go through and just comment on the various things that you may see. Point to them with your finger if you would, or with a pointer, so that we can see what you are talking about. Now, the photograph that you see there, the first photograph in the booklet, what is depicted there and perhaps you might point as you talk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This main building is the new hospital building. This photograph was made now after the war, after the hospital was renewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So it has been rebuilt since 1991. That is what you are saying, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992 it was renewed. The local authorities at that time had rebuilt the hospital, although not fully, but the roof of the central building has been rebuilt. This is the emergency ward, rehabilitation, and here --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would like just -- just perhaps stopping you for a moment to know what the record indicates, you are pointing to the long building with the iron roof in the immediate foreground of the building directly in front of the hospital, the main hospital. Thank you, if you could go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On this lawn was where the white flag with the red cross was. The white sheet, so that one could see that this was a hospital. On the left-hand side --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just stopping you again, Doctor, I will need to indicate these places for the record. This is the green lawn section to the left end of the silver-roofed building, or iron-roofed building first described in front of the hospital. Thank you Doctor, if you could continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, perhaps you can see this destroyed building. It is still destroyed, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is in the medium foreground of the photograph to the left-hand side of the photograph looking at the photograph. Yes, what is that building, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the building of the infectious diseases and test diseases ward and that is where there was a big red cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could you turn to the next photograph, please, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, on this photograph one can also see the central building of the hospital. On the right-hand side is the entrance where the emergency reception room for the wounded was during the war. On the second floor was surgery, and that is where the hospital was first shot at on 15th August from the positions held in Vojvodina and then we moved surgery from the second floor to the first floor, where the gynaecology ward was before that, and soon afterwards, because of the constant shelling, we moved it to the cellar and to the shelter. You can see here these sacks for protection --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, this is in the immediate foreground to the right-hand side of the building, showing the building. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is actually where the reception room for the surgery is, where operations were carried out, and then the wounded were taken through the cellar to the shelter and the shelter is precisely here, underneath this green lawn. That is a real anti-nuclear shelter with four big rooms and with bathroom and storage rooms for water, food, and medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the photograph -- the place on the photograph pointed to is on the left-hand side of the photograph, about two thirds of the way up the photograph, behind a very large tree that is shown there. Thank you Doctor, and moving now, I think, to the next photograph...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here we can also see the main building of the hospital. During those three months while the hospital was a constant target for shelling, all the medical services took place here in the basement, and this was the first floor where internal medicine was, and it is only the medical staff who slept there while the wounded were in the cellar and in the hallway, the central part of the building so there was less of chance for them to get injured again. On the right-hand side up here, that is where a fire broke out. A shell fell and it was precisely on this window that the fire started but we managed to extinguish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Stopping there for a moment, this is the top right-hand side of the building as you see the building, looking at it. Thank you. Now, if we can go on to the next photograph? Is that looking at it again with the entranceway to the hospital where the wounded were brought in which is shown on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the other side now. The wounded were brought in this way, and then an empty vehicle would drive out this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I think if we can move on to the next photograph --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the opposite side of the hospital. The wounded were brought in here. They would be left here in front of the surgery and then the empty vehicle would leave on the other side. Also, you can see here the heating room. The door to the heating room. It is precisely at that place that the head of our heating station, Ivan Ragus was killed. He was getting into the room where he worked and that is precisely where a shell hit him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next photograph? I think we have seen a similar one to that before. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is the second one where the hospital is shown from the side of the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the next photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the entrance to the hallway which is between the old and the new buildings, and this is exactly where the entrance to the anti-nuclear shelter is. It is behind this wall. The medical staff and the wounded and patients from the old building and the new building had access to it. Here, along the hallway there were also beds with patients with the wounded, and this is where they were also treated. On one occasion a shell, an armoured shell had hit the ground, and then hit this wall. So, it was impossible to pass this way and one patient was -- who was not really wounded, he was a tetraplegic from before the war and he was brought to the hospital because his family could not take care of him and we thought that he was killed. However, we managed to dig him out and to re-animate him. He survived all of that, and he is still recovering in Varazdinske Toplice near to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, when you are actually talking, if you could just speak as much as you can into the microphone. I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This photograph also shows the same corridor between the new and the old building, and the entrance into the nuclear shelter. That corridor now is empty but in 1991 it was packed full with the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This photograph shows the entrance to the surgery. This is the anteroom; however, during the aggression of 1991, this room was also used as a surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the door to my office. That was my office during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the final photograph, if you could turn it up, please? Oh no, I am sorry, the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This photograph shows one of the hallways in the hospital that was also used as rooms for patients because we put the beds so that they should be protected by walls without windows because shrapnel would often come through the windows, even whole shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here you see the entrance to the admission, surgery admissions. This was the entrance. The wounded were brought by car and then the cars would continue in that direction. This is how we had boarded-over the windows and covered them with sandbags. The windows of the surgery where the operations were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here you see an entrance to the hospital building from the Gunduliceva Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender those photographs, your Honours. It is next exhibit, in order, P8, I think it will be 8, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Exhibit number 8?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecution exhibit number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, you said that negotiations continued at various levels in order to achieve some sort of cease-fire and in particular to achieve a cessation of the attack upon the hospital. When did those negotiations start in earnest, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall, because I learned of those negotiations from my conversations by telephone with the Health Minister, Professor Doctor Andrija Hebrang, and these negotiations began in earnest at the beginning of October when, as a result of those negotiations, a convoy was organised for the evacuation of the wounded by the Medicine Sans Frontiers, the Doctors Without Borders organisation. This convey was to have reached Vukovar on 11th October to bring medicines and other medical equipment, and to take the first 100 wounded from the hospital and then to keep coming back again until all the wounded were evacuated. The convoy left Zagreb on 11th October but it was held up by the Yugoslav army in the barracks and it did not reach the hospital. The next convoy was organised on 18th October and it did reach the hospital. However it did not bring any medicines at all, not a single pill, but it managed to evacuate 105 wounded in spite of difficulties which resulted in the trip from Vukovar to just behind Vinkovse took 13 hours and an elderly patient who was burned by a shell died during the journey. The negotiations were continued with intensity, and I received the first report that the hospital would be evacuated on 12th November. An agreement had been reached in Zagreb according to which the hospital would be neutralised and the evacuation would begin on November 18th at 8 am, organised by the International Red Cross, under the supervision of the European Monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, I will just ask you to look at this document that I now show you and a copy is to be given to the Defence and to their Honours. Again, it is a document that I have made available to Mr. Fila. Your Honours, I apologise for the difficulty in reading the top section of it, but it is the only copy that we have and the only copy that survived, as far as I know, as far as this office is concerned. Dr. Bosanac, the document you are now looking at, do you recognise that document? Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I have seen it. Actually, I talked on the telephone several times with Minister Hebrang to consult with him regarding the evacuation of the hospital and its neutralisation and I saw this document for the first time when I reached Zagreb after being exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you understand this to be the agreement that was entered into between the parties in relation to the evacuation of the Vukovar hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is an agreement signed on behalf of Croatia by the Health Minister, Professor Andrija Hebrang on behalf of the Yugoslav People's Army by Andrija Raseta, and as the chairman of the European Mission, Georges Marie Chenu.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you recognise any of the signatures that appear at the foot of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And can you tell us which signature you recognise and where that signature appears on the document? Perhaps you might like to put it on the overhead projector and point to it. That might be easier for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is -- I recognise this signature. It is the signature of our Minister, Dr. Hebrang.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is not coming up on the screen, Doctor. I would ask that it be moved up further and if you could point to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the signature of our Minister, Dr. Hebrang. In the middle is the signature of Mr. Chenu, and to the right is the signature of General Raseta.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I take it that you are familiar with the signature of the Minister for Health of Croatia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know this for sure, but as for the other two, I heard that those were signatures of Andrija Raseta. I have not seen his signature. I know that he participated in the negotiations. I spoke to him several times on the telephone in the period between 16th and 18th November, and I know this to be Mr. Chenu's signature because after liberation I spoke to him several times, as after being a member of the Monitors, he had a mandate as the Ambassador of France in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Bosanac, this agreement that was entered into in writing that you have just identified as exhibit 9; what happened in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to that agreement of 18th November 1991 at 8 o'clock in the morning, representatives of the European monitoring mission and two teams of the International Red Cross were due to arrive, one of them by car from Belgrade via Ilok, and the other one across the Danube from Vojvodina. That was the information I received. However, on 18th in the morning nothing happened. Nobody appeared. There were only minor attacks on the town. There were hardly any shells. I went to get water with some colleagues but I saw shells being fired from Vojvodina but far beyond the city, behind the front lines that were held at the time by the Yugoslav army. We were waiting and nothing happened. I call Minister Hebrang up, who said that representatives of the International Red Cross had left Belgrade, that they were on their way. About 12 o'clock representatives of the European Monitors called up by telephone and said that they were on their way to Vukovar, that they were in the village of Negoslavci, and that they still could not come because they were not allowed to come by the Yugoslav People's Army. In the afternoon I called Zagreb up again, that is Minister Hebrang and he told me that the Red Cross had informed him that the teams were in Vukovar, but that they were occupied with the surrender of civilians and the Croatian army, and that they would not come to the hospital before the next day, that is 19th, a Tuesday, at 8 o'clock, and we waited. We had prepared the wounded for evacuation. We made a list where people were going. Those who were on extensions, there were many heavily wounded, they were in plaster casts, and we had to prepare them for evacuation so we engaged in last-minute preparation to begin the evacuation the next day at last. The situation by then was very difficult. There was no medicine or food or water. Gangrene appeared in some cases and civilians started coming to the hospital from the surrounding shelters asking when they would be evacuated, how they could leave the town, along which routes, so that those were the worst days we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were the civilians armed when they came to the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. To the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, they were not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were there any people, any soldiers armed at the hospital during this period, that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that period the command of the defence appointed a group to control the security of the hospital. They had checkpoints outside the hospital, there were six per group. But in the hospital itself there were no weapons, and all the wounded when they were brought in to the hospital at the entrance that I showed you on the photograph, they were totally undressed. Their equipment was removed. A police inspector called Blanko Lugenda had this duty on behalf of the police to register the names of the wounded, to take their weapons and to take them back to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you yourself introduce a policy to prevent weapons being brought into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was strictly prohibited, and when soldiers came to visit their friends, they also had to leave their weapons at the entrance. There was a policeman watching over those weapons, and when they completed the visit they would take their weapons and go away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Bosanac, you have spoken of the fact that the agreed date for the evacuation was to be 18th November in the morning and you have said already that when that day came and that time came and passed, nothing had happened. Can you tell us now what happened after the -- the next thing to occur in relation to the proposed evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day in the morning, again no one came at 8 o'clock, then again I called up the Minister, and he said that Red Cross teams and European Monitors were on the ground, that they expected the evacuation to begin. The Minister himself had gone to Slavonia to meet the convoy. I contacted several people including Minister Granic. I called up General Raseta in Zagreb several times that day to ask him for information. He told me that I should contact Mr. Mrksic who would know exactly how the evacuation would be organised. I could not understand why he did not know where he was, but Raseta told me not to worry. They would find me. The last time I spoke to Raseta, that was Tuesday morning, he told me that according to the information he had, the army had reached the bridge and that the International Red Cross was there too, so I headed towards that bridge, accompanied by Marin Vidic, who was responsible for the evacuation of civilians and an employee of mine who spoke English. She could be used as an interpreter, so we reached the bridge, and we saw in the street called Priljavo between Vukovar and Borovo, many trucks with different troops that was collecting the civilians and loading them into these trucks. We reached the closest personnel carrier carrying soldiers who did not look like soldiers at all because they were wearing different uniforms, they were totally untidy, unshaven, and that was the first time that I really felt scared because this was the first time for me to see such soldiers. I asked for their commander. They were shouting things like, "are you Ustashas", and then one of them appeared as their commander and I asked him for the International Red Cross. He said he had no idea that his territory was as far as the bridge and that he was not going across the bridge, so we went back to the hospital and waited. I do not know exactly what time it was, 12 o'clock, 12.30, a military vehicle arrived carrying soldiers to the hospital and I asked them as well whether they knew where the International Red Cross was and one of the officers said that he did, that he had seen some vehicles with international plates in Negoslovske, so I asked him to take me to Negoslovske. I asked him where Mrksic was. Then he said he was in Negoslovske too, so I asked him to take me to Negoslovske, so I asked him to contact me and see how we could organise the evacuation. He agreed. I also asked him if he could ensure that the troops accompanying him should protect the hospital. People were afraid. There were a lot of civilians in there. There were no international representatives there, and indeed, he ordered the military policeman to guard the entrances to the hospital so I went to Negoslovske for the first time under his escort. I was taken to a civilian house. I later learned that it was probably one of the lawyers' houses, Armicic. An officer was upstairs and he introduced himself as Mile Mrksic. I said I was Vesna Bosanac from the Vukovar hospital and that and I had come for the purpose of evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You have mentioned Mile Mrksic a couple of times. What position did he have, as far as you were aware, at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time I had heard from General Raseta that he was in charge of the operations in Vukovar and that he would contact me in connection with the evacuation. I spoke to him on the telephone once from the hospital, and he also introduced himself as being from Vukovar. I had not known him from before. Actually, I had only heard of him, but I did not know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you understand or know what rank he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know because I am not familiar with ranks anyway, very well. I do not know what rank he had, but later I heard, I think, that he was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you understand him to be connected with or associated with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was commander for that area. Raseta told me that he was the most responsible for operations in Vukovar, and that he would be the one to assist us on the part of the Yugoslav People's Army regarding respect of the agreement on the evacuation of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you spoke -- you went to this place, this house that you said was the former house of a lawyer of the town. What happened then when you were there? Did you meet with Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that he was preparing the evacuation now, and that they still had not decided what route to take, whether via Sid or Adasevci. I protested because it was clearly stated in the agreement that the evacuation would go Lugert, Dogdanovcy, Marince, Luzte, where ambulances and buses were waiting to take over all the wounded, the personnel, all the people who were to be evacuated and I said that we must observe the provisions of the agreement signed in Zagreb. However, he said that that would be very difficult, that it was easy for Raseta to sign the agreement in Zagreb when he was not on the spot, but I insisted on the agreement because we had had problems before with the convoy that had followed the routes, and this was the fastest way to evacuate the wounded and the personnel from Vukovar. Eventually he agreed to follow the route as indicated in the agreement, but he said that certain positions needed to be regulated. He mentioned Zidizne. There were some military facilities there, near the village of Serice. This had to be de-mined first and then the next morning on the 20th the convoy would follow the route to Nustar. This is the conversation we had on Tuesday 19th in Negoslovske.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I take it, Doctor, that you did not have a copy of the agreement with you at the time. You were relying on what you had been told was in the agreement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we agreed that the next day at 8 o'clock the evacuation would begin. I asked whether I could meet with representatives of the Red Cross or the European Monitors, who had called me up on Monday from Negoslovske. He told me that they were busy with the registration of civilians at Velepromet. That was the first time I heard Velepromet mentioned. Then after that they would come to the hospital. I protested. They should come as soon as possible because there was no water or food or anything in the hospital so I went back again accompanied by the same officer, and also this person who went with me for interpretation purposes. I returned to the hospital about 3 o'clock on the same day, and I saw that some assistance had been brought with some water and some canned food. I saw military policemen guarding the entrance, but I also saw some of our employees who had joined the reserve force as volunteers, passing through the hospital, saying hello to some people. The personnel and the wounded were very frightened because these reservists of the Yugoslav army started freely entering the hospital and there were no representatives of the Monitors or the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you mentioned Negoslovske. That was under the control of the JNA at that stage, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And also Velepromet was under the control of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the area around the hospital had just very recently surrendered. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area around the hospital, actually, was under the control of the Croatian police and the defence of the city, but throughout that week we had noticed that the number of troops was declining. They were going to the front, so that in effect the centre of the town was left without any military defences, so that the centre of the town was virtually under the control of the JNA without any major conflicts occurring and when the JNA entered the city centre, the area around the hospital where I was, this happened on the Tuesday 19th in the morning, whereas in the southern sections of the town, the fairgrounds, mitnitsa, the JNA entered that part on Monday 18th, and that is why representatives of the International Red Cross and the European Monitors were there. They were held up there, and that is why they did not reach the centre where the hospital was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And your understanding of the situation was that the International Committee of the Red Cross and the European Community Monitoring Mission people could not get through because of the JNA. It was not a case of them being busy with other matters. You understood the situation as that they could not get through. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what they told me. I personally thought that they did not come because their mandate did not go that far. If they wanted to come they could have come into town to the centre, and to the hospital and I was certain then, and I am certain now that instead of three teams of Monitors and two teams of Red Cross people, if two or three hundred such teams had come directly to the centre of the town, had they come there and stayed there, that they would have prevented the Yugoslav army and the paramilitary units from committing the crimes they did after the war operations ceased in Vukovar. However, regrettably, there were very few of them. They were taken around and manipulated by Major Sljivancanin and others from the army. We saw on cassette Cyrus Vance who was at the hospital on 20th. Slivancinin brought him in and showed him the hospital after the lightly wounded and the staff and everything else was already taken away and when I was already in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. We have moved on a bit, doctor. We will just go back slightly, if we can. You spoke in your evidence of coming back to the hospital after your meeting with Colonel Mrksic and you saw there that there were reservists and other JNA military around the hospital and people were very frightened at seeing this. What was the next thing to occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, for the first time around 4 or 5 pm that afternoon I saw Major Sljivancanin. He entered the hospital yard with a group of soldiers. I was sitting in the hospital with Vesna Zgonjanin who was the representative of the Red Cross and she took care of civilians in Vukovar. She said that there was panic upstairs when they started taking away civilians who had been brought to the hospital in the past two days and that they started separating the men from the women. I went there then because they were taken out of the hospital through the other door on the opposite side of where I had worked and I really saw men being taken away in trucks through the door facing Gondovicovar Street and that is when I first saw this Major Sljivancanin. I saw that he was in command and I walked up to him and I asked him where they were taking these people because first it was agreed upon that the hospital would be evacuated on Wednesday and after that, buses would be sent for civilians. However, afterwards he said that they had to make records of the men, of the civilians, that they had to make lists of them and then they would be returned. This was Tuesday afternoon when they started taking civilians out of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you have been talking of civilians and men. You are talking about people who were actually in the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you, these are people who started coming in as early as Monday, because the evacuation of the hospital was expected on Monday and then of civilians because the shooting had abated. There was no more shelling of the city so they were coming in from their own private shelters, cellars, et cetera, they were all coming to the hospital to find out when they would be evacuated and how so during those two days, Monday and Tuesday, within the hospital compound I am not too sure how many people there were, but almost 1,000, I think. They were there with suitcases, with shopping bags, they were sitting by their wives and their children waiting to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And with respect to Major Sljivancanin, did you ascertain with what organisation he was connected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was also an officer of the Yugoslav army. I do not know exactly what you are referring to. I saw that he had a camouflaged uniform and that he had a cap like the one soldiers wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was the next thing to happen after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taking those civilians away, so the hospital was getting rather empty, because although civilians were upstairs on the first floor and the basement, about 7 pm it was already dark, a truck came of the International Red Cross. Major Sljivancanin had brought in a gentleman, tall, blond. Later on I found out his name was Nikolas, a doctor, and a lady interpreter. They came to the hospital. They brought some medical equipment and medicines in the truck. I was already disappointed by that time, because they did not come all day and I said that we did not need medicines at that point, that we needed evacuation. Then this Nikolas said that this was the earliest he could come, that he brought these medicines and he asked whether we were prepared to evacuate. He went through the entire hospital, and I said that we were prepared two days earlier. We made all the necessary lists, and every wounded person got a little white plastic bag in which the history of his illness was, all his documents, so we were only awaiting evacuation at that point. I was then disappointed in the International Red Cross because this Mr. Nikolas asked me, because we had prepared all of that and Major Sljivancanin brought him in, and whether he could come there the next day at all, whether he should be present during the evacuation. I had understood Minister Hebrang that the International Red Cross would neutralise the hospital and under their control the evacuation would take place. I said that it was not only necessary, but that it had to be so according to the agreement that was signed in Zagreb. He said that he would come in the morning on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they left again. I think they went to spend the night in Belgrade. Again, an officer came to pick me up. I do not know his rank, again, I am not very good with ranks. He had an olive green uniform, not a camouflage uniform, a young-ish man. He came to my office and said that he had received orders to take me to Negoslovske. I got ready. I thought that Mrksic was calling me to come there again because evacuation was being prepared, and as I sat in a car with him and went with him to Negoslovske, I went to the same building and the same room but it was not Mrksic who was there any more but it was Sljivancanin so I saw him once again over there. Also a short man in uniform. I saw him later in the prison in Mitrovica and everybody addressed him as, "captain", but I do not know his name. I was surprised because I was expecting Mrksic and I was asked where Mrksic was and I was told that and he was at a different assignment and they asked me why I was asking and they said that I had already discussed it with him and then Sljivancanin started asking me questions about this, where the Croatian army was, where Jastreb was, where the policemen were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, would you mind slowing down, please, because it is becoming very difficult to interpret what you are saying because you are speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you think that this is the appropriate time for a recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means, your Honours. (A short break)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, before the morning tea adjournment you were telling their Honours that you were taken to a meeting with JNA officers and you had thought that you would be meeting up with Colonel Mrksic but in fact when you arrived there you were surprised to find that Colonel Mrksic was not there and indeed you were confronted by Major Sljivancanin. Now, picking up from that point what happened when you met with Major Sljivancanin on this occasion when you were taken there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin asked me whether I knew who Jastreb was and where he was and where the Croat soldiers were. I said that I did not know, that I was in charge of the hospital, and that I am in charge of preparing the evacuation of the wounded and of the staff. I saw Jastreb and the Croat soldiers for the last time a few days before that when I was preparing a telefax. He was angry and arrogant. He asked who killed his young boys, then, if there was no army there, his young boys who had come to Vukovar, and that -- and I said I was not a soldier and that I did not bring anyone to come and kill people into Vukovar and to destroy Vukovar and I only was in charge of the hospital. That is what I told him. Then I was asked who I was in contact with in Zagreb. A captain threatened me, said that he had all my conversations recorded, and that they could do whatever necessary to indict me. I said that I am not worried about that, that I talked to a lot of people in Zagreb, primarily to the Minister of Health. They were bringing pressure to bear upon me so that I would say where the Croat soldiers were. I simply did not know who had left and when and how. I simply know that the wounded Croat soldiers who were in hospital, I knew them, and that was not a secret. We had kept these records. We treated all the wounded according to all the principles of medicine and ethics and I did not feel guilty at all. I was questioned there for about an hour, and then they told me that I would have to spend that night there in Negoslavci but I requested to be taken back to the hospital but they did not want to. A soldier escorted me from that house to the school in Negoslavci where I saw that was where a hospital was because I saw bedding all over the classrooms. They took me to a room where there were four beds. Those were sleeping quarters.
