utterances.text: "Josip Bradaric - policeman. Was not injured but we cut him and sewed him up so that he could be included among the wounded. He was hospitalised in September 1991 with perforations of the ear. He was called out and taken away and he is registered as missing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This is what you stated when you gave your statement? That is the passage you read out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it customary for doctors to make incisions, to cut patients and then sew them up again? Was that your custom or was this an exception?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have tried to explain the situation and to convey the specific characteristics of the situation as it was at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is, did you have other cases like that of making incisions on patients? Among those who you put in casts, were there many of those? Let me read it out, again, from your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not put on any casts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: "For many, we put bandages and plaster casts so that they would appear to be injured." My question is, were there cases when an old man, or woman or child was given a plaster cast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there any old man, woman or child that was cut or were there not fighters, putting -- who had a guilty conscience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I think that is going outside the context of these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to the reference -- there is no way that this witness knows whether patients had a guilty conscience. I object to that characterisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But the doctor may know whether a woman or a child was being protected or a fighter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence counsel to confine himself to relevant questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In one part of your statement you said: "At that point it was inevitable that the rest of the city would fall. The soldiers surrendered their arms and changed into civilian clothes. Many of them put on bandages or plasters so that it would seem as if they had been wounded." That means that you knew that these people were soldiers who changed their uniforms into civilian clothes, and plaster bandages were put on them so that it would seem as if they were wounded. Is that the kind of medication you provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, you said that you knew about it. Not that you heard it, you knew about it. That is what you said. Are these the people you cut, made incisions on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who was a fighter and who was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This was your statement, madam. Page 3, paragraph 4 from above. Please read it to the Chamber because at that moment -- that is how the sentence starts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wish to add that I do not know who it is and that I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you kindly read what you stated, then to, the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will: "Because the fall of the remainder of the city was inevitable, the soldiers threw away their arms and changed their uniforms into civilian clothes. Many of them put on either plaster or bandages so that they would look as if they were wounded".

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That is what I wished to ask about and now we are going to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a list of patients that the witness provided on this same statement of yours, let me just help you, 5, from the back. That is your list, starting with Crnobrnja. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Number 3. It says, "Bozidar Segec".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: "Member of the ZNG, registered as missing."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Segec.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sorry. They do not have the letter, "Sch", here. I wish to draw the attention of the Chamber to the fact that this Bozidar Segec is not in the indictment provided by the prosecution. "Goran Kovacevic, member of the ZNG". Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: His right eye was injured. First he was registered as missing but I hear that he was exchanged and now he lives -- and this person is on the list of people who were killed. That is how the Prosecutor lists this person. Do you have any knowledge as to whether this person is alive or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you know what you stated here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard and it is assumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, this was just a question. Never mind. Vedran Galic. Do you have any knowledge of him? Number 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I found the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this person? Please read what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Specifically now, at this point in time, I do not know. This was an assumption because it does not say here decidedly that I know. I say, "I believe", that he left Vukovar with the transport and that he now lives nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I do not want to put words into your mouth, doctor. I am simply reading what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Janja Pothorski. You have said that she is a civilian. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian, died during the transport on the road to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the information I had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I wish to draw the attention of the Chamber to the fact that she is listed as killed in Ovcara. Just like the previous four persons. Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, just a few. Doctor, Mr Fila asked you about the head of the ophthalmology department leaving and you indicated that he had left. Did other Serb doctors remain at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And they continued with their duties as normal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they stayed until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And are you aware of anything bad happening to those doctors that stayed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They work in that same hospital until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr Fila asked you about the differences between the way that men and women were treated and the way that fighters were treated. At the time that the JNA came into the hospital, were any of your patients fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were they engaged in combat with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in time nobody was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were the JNA soldiers armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So this is a situation of armed soldiers taking unarmed wounded persons out of the hospital, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr Fila asked you on cross-examination if it was customary for doctors who cut patients who are not injured. Is it customary for soldiers to take patients away out of the hospital and execute them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With your permission, I can perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour, what is this all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Nothing further, your Honour. Your Honour, I would, at this time, though, like to tender the statement of Dr. Striber and just a couple of questions in relation to that. Doctor, you have already been questioned in relation to the statement that you gave on the 14th June of 1995. Do you recall giving that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And at this time I would ask that the witness be shown a copy of the statement in English and if you can, see if you recognise your signature on this document. I would mark this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 13. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is, in fact, your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, your Honour, then, I would tender this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection? I am turning to Mr Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No objection to that, your Honour. However, I do object to the way in which this was put. This should have been done before I cross-examined. In this way, your Honour, the Defence is already unequal because the Prosecutor is entitled to redirect questioning but if it continues this way I am going to give up on my questioning because after my questioning there is a flood of questions, additional questions put by the Prosecutor. It is unfair, and with the permission of this court, I hope the Prosecutor will not mind, it has nothing to do with this, certainly it has nothing to do with this, it is related to the floor plan. The floor plan of the hospital. It has nothing to do with this. I mean, it is not a polemic or anything, it is nothing out of the ordinary. Point 26. What is that? If the Prosecutor agrees, if not, I will withdraw my question. Please, could you just tell me, what is the room numbered 26?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, are you asking this question to our witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: With the permission of the court. There is no contest over this, but it simply has not been explained. What is that room? It is related to the JNA, so that... with your permission, of course, if you allow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If the Prosecution does not object, I would like to ask this question, this question to be asked of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the witness to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I do not believe she has the document in front of her, your Honour. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 26, yes, sir. Put your question and I will answer to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The question is simple. Could you please explain what that room is there? There are no beds there. It says "reservists", so it is not quite clear to me, why are there no beds there, and what period is this related to, because reservists are mentioned, so it is a new point for me. Believe me, it is quite new to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all I did not make the floor plan, so I cannot say why the beds have not been marked here, and why it says, "reservists". I am sorry, but I do not know why you are asking me this question, but as far as I can follow you, I will try to explain. I do not know why it says so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is precisely why I put the question, because they are not quite clear to me. Room 26. As you can see, it is a room without beds. It is a patient's room for reservists of JNA, I imagine, I do not know. JNA reservists. I do not know. Who are these JNA reservists? It is quite unclear what 26 is. So if we can clarify it, let us clarify it. If not, I think that it is the Prosecutor who should clarify it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, at that time we had members of the JNA as patients too. If that relates to that, I imagine that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask the witness simply to clarify, what was in room 26? Can you tell what was there? For what purpose was this room used, if you may remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember beds have not been marked here in room 26, but we did have a few patients who were members of the JNA, and who were staying in the rooms. I cannot state with full responsibility. It says here that this was a room for JNA reservists, but I do not know whether that is a controversial issue here, this notion, "reservists", but this is where the wounded of the JNA army were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, to go back to the objections by Mr Fila, I, with all due respect, would like to clarify that in a way you mixed up two different issues. One issue was whether or not the Prosecutor was entitled to re-examine the witness and ask further questions; this is a basic right of the Prosecution, and each party, any party laid down in our Rules of Procedure. A different issue which you also raised was about the time when a witness statement may be tendered in evidence, and you are suggesting that -- and you would like the -- this statement to be tendered before examination and cross-examination, if I understood you correctly, not after the examination. That is what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am not denying the Prosecutor his right to put additional questions after my cross-examination, but if during the redirect, he asks for the statement to be tendered as evidence, then I can ask no further questions based on that statement because I am not entitled to that. In that way, I am put in an unequal position. That is what I wish to say. I am not denying the gentleman the right to redirect, and he is entitled to that, because I cannot be denied the right to ask questions related to the statement because the statement is tendered as evidence only afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So therefore, as I say, you have the right either to object to the very fact of tendering the witness statement in evidence, or if you accept that it -- that this statement be tendered in evidence, you may wish to -- it to be that this tendering should take place before the examination and cross-examination. If this is your position, we will rule on this matter later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just very briefly just explain, I think that Mr Fila had already asked questions in relation to the statement, so the fact that it was tendered after that in no way affected his ability to ask questions in relation to the statement, and secondly, in this situation it was just an oversight on my part to not tender it during the examination-in-chief. There was no intention to do it at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. I think -- I wonder whether there is any objection to the release -- to our witness being released. Mr Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, because the Prosecutor has said that he had omitted to do that, I withdraw everything I said. If he tenders this on time, in the future, I mean this statement as evidence so in that way I am satisfied with the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. As I say, is there any objection to the witness being released?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you so much for coming to testify and you may be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: While the witness is being released, I will try to -- not to waste our time by raising two issues. First of all, a question to Mr Fila. Mr Fila, you were so kind as to give us this morning a document, actually a set of documents in Serbo-Croatian, including the law on national defence of 23rd April 1982, the law on military service, 2nd December 1985, and the amended law on military service issued on April 26th 1991 taken from the official gazette of the SFRY. Well, we are, of course, grateful to you for giving us these documents. However, we were wondering whether you could point to the court and to the Prosecution the relevant provisions of these laws because we need to have them translated into English and it would be a waste of time and money to translate the whole of these three laws which are really lengthy. My second question relates to the law which we also need, and which I was hoping you would provide us, namely the law on the powers and functions of the various bodies of municipalities in the -- in Croatia at that time. Remember, we asked you to be so kind also as to provide that law. In particular, the provisions of that law relating to the powers of the presidents of municipality, of the assemblies of municipalities. I wonder whether you could, in future, give us this law. And again -- and then before we move on to our next witness, may I come back to an issue raised at the outset by the Prosecutor when the Prosecutor asked the court to allow an investigator, a Prosecution investigator to monitor the hearings, if I understood him correctly. I wonder, before we -- during our recess we discussed this matter. I wonder whether we could get any objection, or the position of the Defence counsel on this issue. I would, of course, before deciding we would need to know what you think about this motion, whether you have any objection about the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not understand why this is needed. If I get an explanation why this is needed, I am certainly going to agree to it but I simply wonder why, so could you explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a provision in the Rules under Rule 90, I believe it is paragraph (E) which allows for this. The reason is that investigators are involved in this case from the outset. They have participated in witness interviews, they do have knowledge of certain facets of the case that may not always be available to all of the investigators -- I am sorry, of all of the attorneys -- so it is helpful at times to have an investigator present who, if a question arises, is able to provide information to us which we believe assists us in presenting the case. Under Rule 90(E) it states: "Notwithstanding subrule (D), upon order of the Chamber, an investigator in charge of a party's investigation shall not be precluded from being called as a witness on the ground that he or she has been present in the courtroom during the proceedings." So the same would apply to Mr Fila, if he has an investigator that he would wish to be present we would certainly have no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I had simply asked for an explanation to understand what was going on but I said in advance that I would agree to it, so fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good. No objection. We will rule --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just explain something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: With the evidence that I provided you perceived all the legislation related to the military in Yugoslavia in the SFRY. That is why there are two laws on conscription, that it would not seem as if I were leaving something behind. All of it has been put there together, however, in addition to all of that, you have the bylaw regulating the municipality of Vukovar where it says exactly what the powers of the municipal assembly are. This has been provided in our submissions on 15th December, and you have the entire organisation of the municipality there, and of course there is no problem involved whatsoever. Of course I can mark the relevant articles if you give me back the documents. I am going to provide this for you by tomorrow. It is no problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. I suggest that we now move on to our next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, Mr Waespi will be taking this next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have just decided that we will grant your request that an investigator be present here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. May I ask the witness to make the solemn declaration? WITNESS M (so declared)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours. This witness has, during the weekend, expressed her wish to have protective measures as to her appearance and she does not want that her face is shown out of this courtroom, but her voice is her voice. It will not be distorted, so I would kindly ask you and the Defence not to address her by her name. As you all know from your statements, the ones we have provided, you and the Defence, her name appears on that, it is not redacted, so I really would like to ask you not to mention the name when you may have questions to her. Good afternoon. Do you feel comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am now retired, but my profession is a certified nurse.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please outline briefly for the court your educational background, very briefly, and your work experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I graduated from the nurses' college, and I worked as head nurse of the department.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Head nurse of which hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hospital in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And for how long have you been working in that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please describe to us in all briefness again the situation and more, the working conditions in the Vukovar hospital in August up to early November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the end of August work in the hospital evolved under absolutely abnormal conditions. One might call them improvised conditions. We could not provide proper facilities. We had to use the same premises for surgery and for accommodation in the case of an attack against the town. At the end of August these attacks became more frequent and we moved into those improvised premises in the basement and in the nuclear shelter. We also ensured reserve quantities of water, food and medicines, and we worked there until the end of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You just mentioned these attacks, that they became more frequent. Was the hospital directly targeted? Do you remember any specific incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hospital was targeted daily. What all of us remember most is the shelling of the hospital which occurred at the beginning of October when an enormous 250 kilogram bomb fell on to the hospital. It fell through all the floors. Fortunately it did not explode. There were several other bombs and this destroyed a building that had already been damaged, so there was less and less space for accommodation. These attacks went on until the JNA entered the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any defence positions out of the hospital -- around the hospital of which you are or were aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no defence in the vicinity of the hospital because that was too far for anyone to be able to hit that far or defend the hospital in that way. It was not possible to do anything in defence of the hospital. If the people were to be around the hospital, they should have had guns or machine guns and that was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where were you living at that time? In the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the staff was in the hospital. Very few staff members could go to their homes or apartments because they were either destroyed or under daily attacks. It was simplest to organise work at the hospital if we all stayed there, so that we avoided leaving the hospital because the question was, if they left, whether they could return which would mean that we would be missing in personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What were your working hours, if I can sort of ask this sort of very sober question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The working hours for all of us were as required. Sometimes 24 hours, 48 hours, our rests were short. It depended on the intensity of the attacks and the number of incoming wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. How many patients in these days in August, September 1991 were in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, there were fewer wounded, that is in August and the beginning of September. There were many wounded coming in, but we could at that time evacuate them to Vinkovci, so that they were daily driven off to Vinkovci. After the end of September this evacuation was no longer possible because Vukovar was surrounded and we had an average of 30 wounded a day until the end of November, newly admitted wounded, but the number at the end was 450 wounded when Vukovar fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What nationality were these patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The patients were all the inhabitants of Vukovar who had stayed there. All the ethnic groups were represented. All the ethnic groups living there; Croats, Ruthenians, Serbs, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there also soldiers among the patients and from each army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were defenders who were wounded on their positions who were defending the town from the aggressors, and there were also several wounded from the aggressor's armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you treat these -- I assume by, "aggressor's army", you mean the JNA army; did you treat the JNA soldiers any different from any of the other patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A patient is always just a patient, and in order to avoid the possibility of any such insinuations one might say that they were even given better treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said just a moment ago that there were no defence lines close to the hospital. Was the hospital itself defended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same way as the whole town. The people who were defending the town thought they were defending the hospital as well. There was no special defence for the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers inside the hospital who would be armed with weapons like machine guns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were no soldiers, nor were there any such weapons. The hospital was guarded by the security to avoid anyone undesirable entering, any acts of sabotage. These were people in police uniforms but without arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was the hospital marked in any way, that it was a hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. On the roof of the hospital there was a big red cross sign, and also in the yard there was a big sheet with the red cross, and these marks could be easily visible from all directions, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I am now going to ask you about the final days of -- at the end of the siege of Vukovar. Is it correct to say that the influx of people into the hospital was for you the signal that Vukovar was about to fall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not normal for as many as 1,000 civilians to come to the hospital in one day, so obviously something was happening in their shelters, so we assumed that the army was very close, and that is why the civilians came to the hospital which, even though damaged, was in better condition than other parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you aware that in those days, middle of November 1991, uniformed men came into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in uniform. Only the wounded came. To enter the hospital they had to have permission. No one came in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you aware of a situation when the son of one of the doctors who was working inside the hospital entered the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Ivankovic's son entered the hospital when we knew that Vukovar had fallen. This was the 18th or 17th, probably 18th November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How did he look like, Mr Ivankovic's son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I saw him he was wearing a camouflage uniform, and he was sitting in a room talking to his parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, on November 18th was there an evacuation planned for the next day, and were there lists made which included the names of all these people who were supposed to be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The evacuation was planned for the 19th, and on the 18th the lists were made of the wounded. The lists of the staff who were divided according to the place they wanted to go to, whereas the patients were classified according to their injuries, so that the number of ambulances and other vehicles could be planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us who drew up these lists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The lists were mostly made by the doctors who had to evaluate the condition of the patients and to envisage evacuation for them. If a patient could not sit, for instance, then he had to be transported in a lying condition and that was the criteria on the basis of which these lists were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was also an administrative aide called Verica Graf involved in drawing up these lists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was involved to the extent that she received the ready list made by the doctors. Her duty was to retype it on the typewriter and to hand it to Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What happened now on 18th November? Did this planned evacuation take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 18th November the evacuation was not planned for the 18th, but for the 19th. On the 18th we were just preparing the evacuation; on the 19th it did not take place, and in the morning we were told that it would be delayed by one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, on 20th November 1991, around 7 o'clock in the morning, were you called by Dr. Kust?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning of the 20th about 7 o'clock, Dr. Kust, the anaesthetist, came to fetch me and said that I was wanted in the surgery department by Dr. Ivankovic so I went there and he was waiting for me together with a doctor who was wearing a JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you later find out what the name of this doctor from the JNA was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned much, much later that his name was Marko Ivezic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there also soldiers in that room as guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. Dr. Ivezic had in his hand a list and he said that the doctor, "wants to examine the patients on this list". Behind me were two armed soldiers, and therefore, the doctor, me, and two soldiers went to look at the patients that he wanted to examine. The first on the list was Josip Bradaric. He was the husband of one of our nurses. We went to see him and the doctor insisted that we unwrap the wound for him to see it. We did that, and he saw that he had a wound on his arm. Then we visited the other patients in haste. We were in a hurry, because the doctor did not insist on examining each and every patient, but he did insist that we do it as quickly as possible. After those examinations we went back to the same spot in the ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How long did this examination of these patients last, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my assessment, about fifteen to twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened next? Were you then called to another meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came back to the surgery admission ward a message was conveyed to us. I do not know whose message it was, whether it was of this doctor, Dr. Ivankovic or somebody else, that all the medical staff must meet in the plaster room. We informed the staff as quickly as we could, but as the hospital is quite large we were meant to congregate there at 8 o'clock. The message that was conveyed at the same time was that all mobile patients should go out into the yard of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who chaired that meeting you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting was chaired by Sljivancanin. He told us, he brought us there to tell us that the medical staff would be evacuated according to plan and that we will do this as we agreed. I do not know who had reached this agreement, the JNA or whoever, but that we would be able to leave that way. That is to say they would ensure buses for us and that we would be moving towards the place that was already written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you describe the way Major Sljivancanin was looking when you saw him that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sljivancanin is a very tall person, so we sort of looked up to him because he was taller than all of us, and he made a political speech to us, I should say. He said that the JNA had many casualties in their aggressor's attack against Vukovar. He said that the war had only started but that he would do his best so that we could leave safely. That he was doing his gladly, but he promised that and that is the way that it would be. And after him Dr. Marko Ivesic spoke to us and he told us that Dr. Bosanac was no longer our director and that he would take over the command over the hospital now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was Sljivancanin wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sljivancanin was wearing a camouflage uniform, and the doctor was wearing a JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned a minute ago that during the time all the hospital staff and the doctors were gathered to attend this meeting, patients and other people were taken out is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. We could not even follow who was leaving and who was ordering these people to leave, so all those who could walk were leaving, irrespective of whether they were children or women or whoever. Only the medical staff could stay in the plaster room. Everybody else had to go out into the yard and it is only later that we received information that out there the men were separated from the women. For example, if the wife have worked in the hospital and her husband was there with him, he would have to go to the other side where the men were taken. That is to say, all the civilians went out, all the administrative aides, all the other staff, all the wounded who could walk, but we who were in the plaster room could not follow all of this. We could not see where they went, and in what direction, what part of town they were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know Marija Bucko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marija Bucko is a nurse who also worked with us at the hospital all the time and her husband was among us with us like all our husbands, or most of our husbands. She believed, because she was one of the last to enter the plaster room, she noticed that they were being taken some place where it was not planned to take them, and when Sljivancanin told us that we would have to be prepared for evacuation she asked where our husbands were and he said that we should make a list of our husbands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was this list --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we -- I mean, another nurse, Marica Mokos this list. She asked us all about our husband's names and this list was given to Sljivancanin, and we did not know where this list was being taken, nor could we think of where our husbands would be taken. After the meeting we took our things and we waited outside in the yard for further evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many names were on that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that list there could have been up to 40 names, between 30 and 40 names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was the name of your husband also on the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you yourself put his name onto that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told the person who was making the list what his name and surname were. She asked me what my husband's name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said a minute ago that after this meeting you went all out of this plaster room into the yard where you were waiting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How long were you waiting there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably until 11 o'clock, approximately. We were told that we should wait for the buses because there were not enough buses, that we should wait there, but still we did not know where all these people had been taken to, and what would happen to us afterwards. In the meantime, ambulances entered the hospital of the JNA army. They went to get the wounded who remained lying in their beds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there, at a certain point in time, one of the husbands coming back with a bleeding nose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one point in time, perhaps around 11 o'clock, from the opposite direction, from the street where we did not expect the buses to come, we were waiting for the buses to come from the other street, the other side. One of the husbands came and his nose was bleeding and he said that our husbands were on a bus in the street opposite to the one where we were waiting, and that is when we went to get them to see where they were coming from and what had happened to them. In the street there was a guarded bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see your husband on that bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. I saw my husband among all these other people. I went to the door of the bus and I told the soldier that my husband was on the bus and that I should like to see him and that he should get out and he said that I should go away and that that would not be allowed, and I went back to the same place. I continued to wait. Some of the husbands had left. Others remained. I went back a few times, so they released him after all. He was perhaps one of the last to leave. A few people remained, and to the best of my knowledge, all of them got out with the exception of two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you approach somebody to ask after the first refusals of these two guards in the bus? Did you approach somebody else who could help you to release your husband? (4.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked Sljivancanin too and he said, "if he is on the bus they will let him go". However, I did not succeed the second time either, and I asked our doctors who were Serbs who stayed on that they helped me, but they said they could not help me but nevertheless he managed to get out somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said a sentence ago that more or less all the husbands were able to be taken off that bus except for two persons. Can you give us the names of those two persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those two persons were our assistant cooks whose wives also worked, Zeljko Jozo and Adaga Jozo. We have not heard of them since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you then board another bus which took off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our husbands who could hardly walk, I should say, we did not know what had happened to them, they were terrified. They did not say anything. They joined us, and according to instructions, we went to wait for the buses that were supposed to come and collect us. We were waiting for them perhaps some time between 1 and 2, about 1.30 the buses arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many buses did arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four or five buses arrived. One bus was prepared to take the people who wanted to go to Serbia. There was plenty of room there because only a few people boarded that bus because all the rest wanted to go to Croatia. I forgot to mention that Sljivancanin in his speech said that we could ask to go to Croatia but Croatia was not willing to take us. That was a gesture that surprised us because we were sure that our people were waiting for us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Which direction, which route, did the bus take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little below the hospital, near the court building. The buses were parked, and when we got on them, the buses passed through the very heart of the city through Radica Street, Senowa Street, in the direction of Negoslavci. We stopped for the first time near the Velepromet building. I do not know why we stopped there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps your Honours, I see it is 4 o'clock, I have some more questions. It would be a convenient time for having a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. All right. We stand in recess for twenty minutes. (4.05 pm) (A Short break) (4.20 pm)

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the point of clarification, we should pass this written note, the name to the witness because, as you are aware, she only recently asked us for this type of protection, so we need to assign her a pseudonym, so I would like to ask the usher to give this piece of paper with her name on it to her, and ask her whether that is her name. (Handed). And not to say the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And show it to the Defence, please, and then to the judges. I would like to tender it afterwards as exhibit number P14 under seal. Thank you, your Honours. Further on, this witness will be referred to as letter M. Thank you. Just before the break you said that the bus stopped at Velepromet. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The bus stopped at Velepromet, but not one of us asked to leave the bus. Why we were stopping there, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How long did you stay at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not long. Maybe fifteen or twenty minutes, then we went in the direction of Negoslavci, but in the meantime we turned in the direction of the Modateks factory. We thought we were going towards Bogdanovci because that was the direction and that was how we thought our evacuation would take place, but shortly afterwards we turned back again in the direction of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you were again on the road from Vukovar to Negoslavci. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were going in the direction of Negoslavci. We were stopped very often. Various vehicles belonging to the JNA passed by us. The reason for the stops we did not know, but when we saw that convoy of ambulances pass by us, we realised that that was what we were waiting for, for the ambulances to go in front, and then the column proceeded towards Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, besides these ambulances there was not much traffic. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In our direction, no. We were alone, but there were vehicles coming in the other direction, JNA vehicles. When it got dark we noticed that the vehicle in front of us was a military vehicle with its lights on. Also, at the end of the column there was another vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you finally arrived in Negoslavci, was it already dark? Was that the moment when you realised that there were lights on the front car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We realised only when dark fell, and this must have been about 4 or 5 o'clock in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How was the general condition of that road between Vukovar and Negoslavci? Was it easy to roll on with your bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no problems whatsoever, except for these stops which were never explained to us. We would ride for a couple of kilometres and then stop and then go on and that is how we got to Orolik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You just said that you got to Orolik, so you -- after Negoslavci you continued on the road to Orolik. Was this kind of road any different to the one between Vukovar and Negloslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no difference. Only when we reached Orolik we thought again we would be going towards Vinkovci but we did not. We went towards Sid. The whole column of buses turned off towards Sid....

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was your final destination that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not know what our final destination was, but after some time we found ourselves in Sremska Mitrovica. We did not know why we were taken there and in the centre of Sremska Mitrovica the buses stopped. We could get off, and that was when I saw for the first time that we had been joined by European Monitors who said, who told us not to leave the buses. We asked where the other people were, those who left the hospital much before us. We thought that we would meet them there. However, there were only our buses there, and they warned us that we should list the people who we thought had been taken somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like now to leave these events in November 1991. You gave an interview to one of -- or several of the investigators of this office on 19th and 20th June 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sure. You talked to one or two persons from the International Criminal Tribunal, this court, in June 1995. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you signed a document at the end which reflected the testimony, or the interview you gave. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would now like the usher to hand over the English version of the statement to the witness, and have her asked whether those signatures here at the bottom of each page is her signature. It would be Prosecution exhibit number 14, marked for identification, probably A if we later have the Croatian version as well. Do you remember having -- is that your signature on all these pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like, your Honours, to tender that statement now into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection from the Defence? No, so it will be A, I understand, because the B will be the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, the original version which is the English version would be Exhibit 15, and the translation into Serbo-Croatian would be 15A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. No further questions. Thank you. Mr Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, witness, you were in the hospital. Do you know, because Dr. Bosanac has already testified that already, on the 19th some people were taken from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Two of our medical technicians, Marko Mandic, Juderic Slatko and another worker, Marko Valaho were taken on the 19th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was any person among them who was later missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marko Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And nothing is known about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is there any information that one of them ended up in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In connection with Bradaric, you said that the doctor undid the bandage, was it on his hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether it was his right or left arm. The doctor asked the bandage to be removed. We removed the bandage, and of course, the doctor saw a wound, an injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you make that injury? Was it made in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can an injury be caused in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The witness before you said that this injury was made in the hospital, that the doctors had cut him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot claim that. I do not know. I was the person who undid the bandage. In fact, it was not even me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you cannot claim that it was not done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot claim either.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Because you have asked me how come this could happen, and I am explaining to you how. You were present when the army entered, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In certain segments, yes, partly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did anyone come, people from Vukovar, local people, with them? You mentioned Ivankovic and others. It is stated in the statement,?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The day before on the 19th in the afternoon; Bogdan Kuzmic came to the hospital who was looking for one of our nurses. Then there was Sascha Maksemovic, Dudzko Cucovic. I saw him in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean that they could have shown the JNA where things were in Vukovar? How else could they have known where the hospital was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were people working in the hospital. Cucovic was working in the hospital. Bogdan Kuzmic too was working in the hospital so they knew exactly where the hospital was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they know what Vukovar looked like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Of course, when they are from Vukovar. So there was no need from somebody from the outside to come and show them the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I cannot tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see anyone else showing them things? Did you see yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not see any persons from outside Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have some very brief questions regarding the 20th. Can you tell us roughly what time you reached the Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we left about 1.30 in the direction of Velepromet, then I do not think the drive could have lasted more than -- of course very approximately it could have been 1.30 or 2, so we were not later than 2.30 there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. So it was still daylight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did dusk, begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was already dusk, when we were not going towards Negoslavci, but while we were stopping... I cannot tell you exactly how much time we spent in front of Velepromet, then we took a different road, then, as far as I remember, it was dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you reached Negoslavci, you got there eventually.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You have to pass Negoslavci to get to Orolik.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was it dark when you get to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was still dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It was still dusk. And in Orolik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Orolik it was already dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During your journey did you see the army? Were there any barricades, tanks, or anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were no barricades across the road, but our buses would stop. Do not ask me what vehicles they were. Some kind of weaponry. They were going in the opposite direction from us. They were going towards Negoslavci and Vukovar and we were going in the opposite direction. This was probably one of the reasons why we stopped from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All the other vehicles following you would also have to stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So can we conclude from this that in the course of your drive from Velepromet to Negoslavci and Orolik you saw the army from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do not be concerned. That is all I want to know. Thank you. I have another problem -- just one more question, and then perhaps we can deal with the problem. If I were to show you a video of those buses, could you tell whether it was on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether I could tell by seeing the tape, but I know for sure that it was the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, when you were there I believe you but could you tell if you were to be shown a tape? Have you seen any videotapes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, but just to clarify that also this statement is under seal, the one we just handed as exhibit Prosecution number 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just one minor question. I wonder whether -- you mentioned -- I am turning to the witness. You mentioned Josip Bradaric and you saw him. Was he a relative of one of the members of the hospital staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the husband of one of our nurses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether there is any objection to the witness being released. No objection? No objection? Thank you so much for coming here. You may be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I am turning to the Defence counsel and asking whether -- you said that you would raise an issue, a general question, Mr Fila. A problem, or whatever, a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Would you like now, since we have some time?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a general question. The video that was referred to at the closed session shows this, so I am asking how can we deduce from that -- you know which video I am referring to, in connection with the alibi. Could she identify whether those were the buses that she was in? I am asking how we could do that, and whether we could do that so as to be sure that that was taken then, so I would suggest that the Prosecutor do this in private session, if he wishes to. I think that would be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a very simple process of the televisions outside being turned off for very short segments for this. It can happen very easily and it is technically not complicated to do, so if Mr Fila ever feels that he would like to show the video he should simply ask for it to be in private session and I think it takes minutes for them to flick switches up in the control booth and he can do that quite safely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr Fila? Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I agree, but the Prosecutor has the video. I have nothing to show and that is the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will certainly make it available. I should say, yes, Mr Williamson has indicated and suggested to me, if Mr Fila would feel that he would like to put this video to this witness that has just been here, we certainly have no objection to getting the tape for him, making it available and for this witness to be recalled so that he may do that, if he feels that he would like to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Your Honour, it is just the end of the video. You have two or three minutes. If you recall, it is the departure of the buses that is shown. The last two or three minutes. That is all, if you are agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it is a question of timing. I wonder whether -- how long it would take you to provide the technicians with the videotape and then show it in private session or otherwise we could put it off until tomorrow and meanwhile hear another witness, start with another witness. But then you would have to ask the witness who came before not to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know what arrangements have been made for the witness to leave. I have a feeling that the witness might be planning on returning tomorrow morning early. I think there was some plans for them to fly back, the three women to fly back. What I might suggest to your Honours is that if we start with our witness now, and then just before the break, say at about quarter past, in the meantime we could have people organise it so that the witness could be brought back and for fifteen minutes that could be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes. If it is agreeable to you, yes. Good. To Mr Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I agree. I would even agree if one of the members of the Prosecution team show the video to the witness and then tell us what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. That is very kind of you but it cannot be done. So we will proceed with the witness number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this next witness has requested full protective measures which would include a pseudonym, image alteration and voice alteration so I understand that we would have to take a break anyway in order to implement the voice alteration. In the time that we do that, we could have the video down here and just show it to this witness, so I would perhaps suggest that we just put this next witness off until in the morning and we can conclude with the last witness and show them the video, if that is acceptable to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have now to have a recess of about 10 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: As soon as we can get the tape down here. It may even be five minutes, your Honour. It will be very brief. (4.40 pm) (A short break) (5.00 pm) (In closed session) (Witness M entered court)
